newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish punt steady as dust clears after sell-off.
newsitem.headline: Irish punt steady as dust clears after sell-off.

text.p: The Irish pound was steady in early trade on Thursday after plummeting the previous day when it came under fierce selling pressure because of concerns that its high exchange rate in the ERM was unsustainable.

Dealers said the punt's fall of more than four pfennigs on Wednesday was probably enough to stem more selling in the short term, but in the long term it faced the same problem -- a market belief that it will enter a single currency at its central ERM rate of 2.4111 marks, more than 14 pfennigs below its current level.
By 0740 GMT the punt was trading at 2.5572 marks compared with 2.5566 in late trade on Wednesday. It was at 0.9170 stg versus 0.9180, and $1.5100 versus $1.5110.
"I don't think the pressure on the punt will go away," said Dan McLaughlin, chief economist at Dublin's Riada Stockbrokers.

"You might see a little bit of a bounce -- we fell four pfennigs yesterday and in that sense you might get a short term bounce," he said. "But the fundamental problem is still there -- the perception is that at the start of 1999 the authorities want it at its central rate of 2.41."
The Irish pound appreciated dramatically in the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) grid in the second half of 1996 and early 1997, pulled higher by a resurgent sterling.
But many analysts believe that if Ireland joins economic and monetary union (EMU) in January 1999 it will want to do so at its central ERM rate, not its current high levels.
Although the possibility of the punt being revalued in the ERM to give it a higher central rate has been mooted by some economists, many dismiss it.
"I doubt very much if the Irish authorities would ask for a revaluation," McLaughlin said.
Dealers said selling pressure might have been exhausted in the short term, however.
"We should see the Irish pound consolidate here," one Dublin dealer said. "What we saw yesterday was huge selling of the punt and buying of the Finnish markka."

Wednesday's sell-off was the second time in a month that the Irish pound had been sent into a spin because of a market belief that it must fall against the German currency before Ireland's EMU membership.

Three weeks ago the pound plunged against the mark in what dealers said was a reaction to the Irish finance minister's televised comments that he would like to see it closer to its central ERM values.
The Central Bank of Ireland was forced to raise interest rates by half a point on May 1 in a surprise move aimed at stemming the punt's fall.
McLaughlin said the inflationary implications of the punt's tumble on Wednesday could spur another rate rise.

"The problem is that the trade-weighted index went down nearly two percent yesterday. If that continues -- in other words, if we're falling both against the mark and sterling -- they may react," he said.
"Just to deal with the domestic inflationary implications, you wouldn't rule out another half point (rise) in official rates. But I think they might wait to see before they do anything."
